extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers preparing tables and managing rights/permissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing, formatting, editing, and publishing tables (and related illustrations), plus basic rights/permissions/copyright rules relevant to reproducing and licensing tabular or illustrated material. Targets preparing tables for print and electronic publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of column heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Column heads that share a row align on the baseline; if any head occupies more than one line, all the heads in that row align on the last (lowest) line. Each column head except in the stub column is normally centered on the longest (i.e., widest) cell entry. If the longest entry is unusually long, adjustment may be necessary to give an appearance of balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If centering does not work, align column heads (see figs. referenced). Ensure visual balance; consider alternate alignment when a single long cell entry skews centering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stub head and entries alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The stub head and entries are always aligned on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stub entries and their head must align left so rows are clearly associated with their stub.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of numbers within columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a column, numbers without decimal points are usually aligned on the last digit (ranged right). If the numbers include decimal points, they are typically aligned on the decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For quantities less than 1.0, zeros before the decimal need not be added in a table unless a journal/style prescribes it. Where spaces rather than commas separate digit groups, align on the implicit comma. Center the column of numerals within the column on the longest (widest) numeral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose predominant alignment when column has mixed number types
rubrics_metrics.description: A column including different kinds of numbers is best aligned on the ones that occur most frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: most values aligned on decimal point while N values centered. Consider frequency and reader comprehension when choosing alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of ellipses and em dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses and em dashes are centered within their cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow fig. examples for consistent placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment for columns of words/phrases/sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: When a column consists of words, phrases, or sentences, appearance governs left-right alignment. If no runover lines are required, entries may be centered. Longer entries usually look better if they begin flush left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runover lines may be indented or, if enough space, aligned flush left with the first line. Choose alignment that improves readability and appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for totals, averages, and means
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra vertical space or short rules sometimes appear above totals at the foot of columns but should not appear above averages or means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency and follow journal/series style. The word 'Total' in the stub is often indented; treat subtotals similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to include totals and subtotals
rubrics_metrics.description: Totals and subtotals may be included or not, according to how useful they are to the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When percentages in a column are based on different n’s, a final percentage based on the total N may be informative and should be included if so. If rounding causes the percentage total to be slightly off (e.g., 99% or 101%), give the actual value or explain in a footnote if the total is reported at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and placement of notes to tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes to a table are of four general kinds and, where two or more kinds are needed, should appear in this order: (1) source notes, (2) other notes applying to the whole table, (3) notes applying to specific parts of the table, and (4) notes on significance levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes always appear immediately below the table (as table footnotes) and must be numbered separately from the text notes. Multipage-table exceptions: if no general notes and specific notes pertain only to a single page, those notes may appear on that printed page; in electronic formats, notes are usually grouped at the bottom with links to references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging data in source notes to tables
rubrics_metrics.description: If data for a table are not the author’s own but are taken from another source, full acknowledgment must be made in an unnumbered footnote introduced by Source or Sources in italics and followed by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shortened form may be used if the sources are listed in the bibliography. Unless fair use applies, reproducing a table without change from a published work under copyright requires formal permission; credit should be given in a source note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes applying to the whole table
rubrics_metrics.description: A general note applying to the table as a whole follows any source note and is introduced by the word Note in italics and followed by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the substance is brief it may be added parenthetically to the title. Scientific publications sometimes use headnotes immediately after the title to expand or qualify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes to specific parts of a table (reference symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: For notes that apply to specific parts of a table, superior (superscript) letters, numbers, or symbols may be used; one system should be used consistently across all tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior letters are generally preferred, but choice depends on context: numerals for tables of words, symbols for tables with equations. Each table should have its own series of notes (beginning with a, 1, or *), sequence runs left-to-right top-to-bottom, and the same symbol may be used on multiple elements if the note applies to them. The reference mark is repeated at the foot beginning the corresponding note and may be followed by a space but never a period. When symbols are used, follow the given sequence (*, +, dagger, double dagger, §, ||, #), doubling when more symbols are needed. Do not use asterisk as a reference mark if p values occur in the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes on significance levels (probability notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a table contains notes on significance levels, asterisks may be used as reference marks: one asterisk for the least significant level, two for the next, three for the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than three levels are given, use footnote letters instead of asterisks to avoid misleading the reader. In the note, the letter p (probability) is usually lowercase and italic; zeros are generally omitted before the decimal point. Probability notes follow all other notes and may be set on the same line or separated by semicolons if spaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing table content for style and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should be edited for style, with special attention to capitalization, spelling, punctuation, abbreviations, numbers, and use of symbols. Check internal consistency, consistency across multiple tables, and consistency with the surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations used in tables should be clear from the table alone; totals and discrepancies must be checked and referred to the author; verify footnote references and correct sequence of letters/symbols; check tables for relevance to text and redundancy with other tables. A lay reader or nontechnical editor should be able to make logical sense of a table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'percent' versus 'percentage'
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago style regards 'percent' as an adverb (or less commonly an adjective) and 'percentage' as the noun form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The symbol % may stand for either word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number ranges must be precise and non-overlapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure number ranges do not overlap, have no gaps, and are as precise as the data require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear whether 'up to' means 'up to' or 'up to and including.' Use dollar ranges consistently (e.g., 'less than $5; $5–$9; $10–$14'). Use < and > only for 'less than' and 'more than'; for ages, '>60' means more than 60 years old. Insert correct symbols for = and ≤; do not underline to indicate symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and symbols in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In a column consisting exclusively of, for example, dollar amounts or percentages, the signs should be omitted from the cells and included in the column head (or occasionally in the stub entry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical operational signs preceding quantities in a column of numbers are not necessarily aligned with other such signs but should appear immediately to the left of the numbers to which they belong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of N versus n
rubrics_metrics.description: An italic capital N is used to stand for the total number of a group; an italic lowercase n stands for a portion of the total group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: N for total subjects, n for number of males or females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting long and narrow vs wide and shallow tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, narrow tables (few columns, many rows) and very wide tables (many columns, few rows) may not work in print; remedies include doubling up (two halves side by side with repeated column heads), turning the table (make stubs the column heads), doubling up again, or presenting broadside (rotated 90°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long tables, specify whether 'continued' lines and repeated column heads are allowed and where footnotes should appear. Choose the arrangement that preserves readability and fits page constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for oversize tables
rubrics_metrics.description: If an oversize table cannot be accommodated with previous remedies, further editorial or typographic adjustments are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorten wording, use abbreviations, omit running head when a table takes a full page, extend slightly into margins, reduce type size, publish electronically only, use numbers for column heads with definitions in notes, or turn column heads on their sides. Consider reader convenience when choosing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking rules (lines) and spanner rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should ensure that rules appear as needed and that spanner rules are the right length and distinct from underlining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that rules will appear as actual rules (not italicized text) in the typeset version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify and check alignment of numbers and text
rubrics_metrics.description: Alignment of rows and columns must be clearly specified in the manuscript; editors should check that numbers have been aligned properly (e.g., by decimal point) and that stub entries correspond to rows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear instructions in manuscript to avoid layout errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid old-style numerals in tabular matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Old-style numerals, though elegant in text, should be avoided in tabular matter because they do not align horizontally as well as regular 'lining' numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If old-style numerals must be used, choose a font that includes a fixed-width 'tabular' version to ensure vertical alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running heads on full-page and multipage tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Running heads should be omitted on full-page and multipage tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor must confirm omission, with exceptions referenced (see other sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking typefaces and markup against design
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers set typographic style for tables; journals follow their established style. Editors should ensure tables are edited in accord with the design and that formatting/markup for electronically prepared tables is consistent and correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check markup, fonts, and other typographic treatments against the publication's style and design specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables of more than one page ('continued' tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a vertical table of more than one page, repeat column heads on each page. For a two-page broadside, column heads need not be repeated; for broadside tables beyond two pages, repeat column heads on each new verso.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where column heads are repeated, include the table number and 'continued.' Editor should specify whether continued lines and repeated column heads are allowed and where footnotes should appear (usually at the end of the table as a whole). Omit running heads on full-page/multipage tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accessibility for electronic tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers concerned about accessibility should ensure proper table markup for electronic formats to enhance accessibility for readers who use text-to-speech and related tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render tables as marked-up text rather than images where possible; if images are necessary or table is especially complex, provide alternative text. Consult DIAGRAM Center, WAI (W3C), and EPUB accessibility guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright basics: relevant law and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For most publishing purposes the relevant law is the Copyright Act of 1976 and its amendments; the chapter provides a basic knowledge of how copyright is acquired, owned, what it protects, duration, and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an overview, not legal advice; other countries' laws may differ despite treaties like the Berne Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: How copyright arises (fixation and original expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a work is fixed in a tangible form and embodies original expression it is automatically covered by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible includes electronic memory; broadcasting without recording is not fixed. Original expression (selection and arrangement) has a low threshold—a modicum of creativity is sufficient. Facts, ideas, and theories are not protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and notice (recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration with the U.S. Copyright Office is advisable but not a prerequisite to legal protection; copyright notice is no longer required but is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration has practical benefits (discussed elsewhere); any work protected under U.S. law can be registered, including certain foreign works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship categories: individual, joint, collective
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish individual authorship from joint works (two or more authors intending their contributions to be merged) and collective works (independent contributions compiled—copyright in selection/arrangement belongs to compiler separate from component copyrights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: journal articles often joint; anthologies are collective works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works made for hire: categories and written agreement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Works made for hire treat the employer or commissioning party as the author. Three categories: works prepared within scope of employment; works by an agent deemed an employee by control factors; and specially ordered or commissioned works when both parties agree in writing and the work falls in specified categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only certain types of commissioned works qualify (e.g., contributions to collective works, motion-picture contributions, translations, instructional texts, tests, atlases, compilations, supplementary works). The written agreement must expressly say 'made for hire' (can be retroactive but safer to sign beforehand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligible works for 'made for hire'
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works cannot be treated as works made for hire regardless of agreement—e.g., monographs and novels are ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright in such works remains with the writer unless expressly assigned; assignment differs from work-for-hire in implications for duration and termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authorship effect on work-for-hire term
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one of a group of coauthors is writing on a 'for hire' basis, the resulting joint work will be treated as made for hire for copyright duration purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can affect copyright term even if other coauthors are independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of the copyright owner (bundle of rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial owner possesses rights of reproduction, distribution, and public display; these rights may be transferred individually or as a bundle to a publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online publication blurs reproduction and distribution; transmission on demand may constitute reproduction/distribution and display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative works and performance rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright includes the right to make derivative works (translations, abridgments, dramatizations, adaptations); revised editions typically qualify as derivative works with separate copyright. Public performance rights have limited relevance for literary works but apply to other media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand distinctions when licensing and assigning rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rights and copyright management information
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators of certain works of fine art have moral rights against mutilation and misattribution; federal law also protects the integrity of 'copyright management information' (CMI) such as title, author, copyright owner, terms and conditions, and identifying numbers or links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law prevents intentional removal/alteration or use of false CMI if done with intent to induce or conceal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark protection for titles and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying only a title is unlikely to be copyright infringement, but a title may acquire trademark protection under federal or state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book titles are harder to protect as trademarks than journal titles; some titles (e.g., Gone with the Wind) are protectable while books remain under copyright; names of characters or locales may also gain trademark protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic vs subsidiary rights and their administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The copyright holder can exercise basic rights (reproduce/distribute) and also license subsidiary rights (other languages, audio, motion-picture). Publishers typically administer subsidiary rights and permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsidiary rights often involve specialized markets and may be licensed to third parties; authors (especially trade authors) may retain some subsidiary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author responsibilities for permissions and acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: If data or material are taken from other sources, authors must obtain permissions where required and acknowledge sources in table source notes. Permissions (licensing photocopies/scans, reproducing illustrations) are part of subsidiary-rights work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless fair use applies, reproducing a table from a published work requires formal permission and credit in a source note. Publishers often handle permissions, but authors may need to obtain them in some arrangements.
